passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text: Temporary remote work means working for a period from somewhere other than your usual work location, such as a family home or a holiday rental, while doing your normal job. Travelling to do Ridgeline work at a client, a project site or another Ridgeline office is business travel, not temporary remote work; see RSE-LOC-01 §2.

passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text:
Temporary remote work within the state or province of your usual work location is allowed. Tell your manager where you'll be working.
No approval is needed, but you must still meet core hours and, if you are office-hybrid, plan around your anchor days. For example, an Austin employee spending a week working from family in another Texas city just tells their manager.

passages.title: Approval Matrix
passages.text:
Request | Approver
Temporary remote work, same state/province | None (tell your manager)
Temporary remote work, other US state/province, up to 30 calendar days/year | Manager
Temporary remote work, other US state/province, over 30 calendar days/year | HR
Working from another country (any length) | HR (Cross-Border Review)
Change to remote-approved | Manager + HR
Business travel | Manager
The rules behind these rows are in the Remote & Hybrid Work Policy (RSE-RW-01) and the Work Location, Travel & Cross-Border Work Guidelines (RSE-LOC-01). Requests to work from another country go to HR's Cross-Border Review through an HR ticket; a manager's support is welcome but is not an approval.

passages.title: Work Location, Travel & Cross-Border Work Guidelines
passages.section_heading: Business travel vs temporary remote work
passages.text:
Travel to do Ridgeline work at a client, a project site or a Ridgeline office is business travel, not temporary remote work. A business trip of up to 14 calendar days needs no Cross-Border Review, even when it is to another country. Longer stays, or working from another country for your own reasons, follow §3.
For example, a week at the Toronto office for project meetings is business travel for a Denver employee: the manager pre-approves it and no Cross-Border Review is needed. Spending several weeks working from a family home abroad is not business travel, even if you do your normal job while there.

passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text: When working remotely, be available during core hours, 10:00–15:00 in your local time zone, as in the office (RSE-HB-01 §3.2).

passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text:
Temporary remote work from another US state, or another province, needs your manager's approval for up to 30 calendar days per calendar year in total. Anything over 30 calendar days in a year needs HR review: your manager can't approve it alone, and HR decides.
The 30 calendar days count every day you are away, including weekends, and they add up across all trips in the calendar year. For example, a stay from the first of one month to the tenth of the following month is well over 30 calendar days, so it needs HR review even if your manager supports it. Submit the request in the HR Portal with your dates and location; HR reviews longer stays because working in another state or province can affect payroll and tax registration.

passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text:
Working from another country always needs HR review, whatever the length. See RSE-LOC-01 §3 for the rules and the Cross-Border Review.
Your manager can support the request, but cannot approve it. Plan well ahead: the review takes time, and there are notice and security requirements before you go.

passages.title: Remote & Hybrid Work Policy
passages.text:
Field/site-based employees are not eligible for temporary remote work.
Their work depends on being at the project site. Travel to another site for work is business travel (RSE-LOC-01 §2).
